lead: Virtual reality did not begin in 2016 on a shop shelf. It arrived in three waves: flat-picture depth experiments and moving cockpit trainers before computers; a laboratory era in the 1980s and 1990s that built the first tracked head-mounted displays and gave the field its name; and a consumer wave from 2012 that pushed the same parts into cheap factory-made hardware. The waves explain why each part of a VR system exists (see 1.5), and they stop you from handing the whole invention to one person.
prereq: You need: 1.1 for the terms VR and virtual environment.

blocks.text: The first piece of VR was a viewing instrument: two drawings seen through lenses or mirrors, one for each eye. In 1838 Charles Wheatstone described the stereoscope: two drawings of one scene, made from viewpoints a little apart, one for each eye. The brain fuses the pair into a single object with depth. The lesson is large — depth needs no solid object, only two correct flat views. Every stereo headset still uses this trick; the display hardware is in Unit 3, Stereoscopic display technology.

The second half of VR is the loop: the user acts, the machine answers. Flight trainers supplied it. From the 1920s and 1930s, trainers such as Edwin Link's put a trainee inside a mock cockpit on a moving platform. The pilot read instruments and moved the controls; the rig tilted in reply. Nothing was drawn on a screen, yet the body felt motion and the pilot made real decisions, while an instructor watched and scored without risk.

In 1962 Morton Heilig patented the Sensorama, a booth for one person. It played stereo film with stereo sound, tilted and vibrated the seat, blew wind at the face and released smells. It worked, but the film was fixed: the viewer could not look elsewhere or change events. What it added was multisensory presentation — proof that one machine can address eye, ear, skin and nose together.

sections.h3: The laboratory era names the field

blocks.text: In 1965 Ivan Sutherland wrote a short essay on the ultimate display. A screen, he argued, should be a window into a world the computer builds, not a surface with marks on it. He pushed the idea to its edge: a display could, in principle, control the existence of matter in a room. That was a target, not a product, and the field chased it for fifty years.

In 1968 Sutherland's group built the first head-mounted display whose computer-generated image was driven by head tracking. Two small cathode-ray tubes, one per eye, showed the computer image. A mechanical arm measured where the head pointed. Displays and arm hung from the ceiling above the user, which is why the rig is remembered as the Sword of Damocles. The important part was the loop: turn your head, and the image turns with you. That loop, not the helmet, is what makes it VR; 1.4 explains why.

VPL Research, founded by Jaron Lanier in the 1980s, sold the hardware that made the idea famous. The DataGlove measured how the fingers bent, so a hand could act inside the world. The EyePhone was its head-mounted display. VPL also popularised the phrase virtual reality, which then displaced the older names used for the same idea.

NASA's VIEW system in the late 1980s put a head-mounted display, a glove, head tracking and the computer driving the scene into one working machine for astronaut training and remote operation — the parts of 1.5 working together. In 1992 came the CAVE: a room whose walls are projection screens, viewed through stereo glasses by several people at once, with no helmet. In 1995 Nintendo's Virtual Boy, a red monochrome display on a stand, proved uncomfortable to use and sold badly.

In 2012 Palmer Luckey's Oculus Rift raised money on Kickstarter. It used cheap phone-grade motion sensors, a wide field of view and a low price. Developer kits reached thousands of programmers, and the field restarted after a quiet decade.

In 2014 phone-based viewers arrived: a phone as the screen, two plastic lenses, a cardboard or plastic shell. They cost very little and put stereo VR into millions of hands, but their tracking was poor. In 2016 consumer headsets reached shop shelves, with tracked hand controllers and room-scale tracking.

A few headsets around 2016 began to place cameras on the headset itself (inside-out tracking), so the headset watched the room and needed no external boxes. The first widely sold headsets of that year still used external cameras or base stations; inside-out tracking became the norm in standalone headsets a few years later. Unit 2 covers how such a tracker measures orientation.

items: Wave 1, before 1965: depth from two flat views, motion cueing, several senses at once.
Wave 2, 1965 to the 1990s: the tracked head-mounted display, the sensing glove, the name, the shared room.
Wave 3, 2012 onwards: low cost and wide field of view from the start, inside-out tracking arriving later in the wave, factory-scale production.

figure.caption: Six landmarks on one timeline. Upper row: the Sensorama booth, Sutherland's tracked display, the CAVE and the consumer headsets that began with the Rift campaign. Lower row: VPL's DataGlove and inside-out tracking. Notice the long gap in the upper row between the 1968 display and the 1992 CAVE.

spec.aria: A timeline in years with two rows, one for display landmarks from the Sensorama booth to consumer headsets, one for interaction landmarks, with the consumer headset bar and the inside-out tracking bar highlighted.

examples.question: Four VR landmarks are given: the CAVE, the Oculus Rift Kickstarter campaign, Sutherland's tracked head-mounted display, and the Sensorama. (a) Arrange them oldest first with the year of each. (b) Find the gap in years between each consecutive pair. (c) State the largest gap. (d) In one line each, say what the landmark added.
steps: Collect the years: Sensorama 1962, Sutherland's tracked head-mounted display 1968, CAVE 1992, Oculus Rift Kickstarter 2012.
Sort by year: 1962 < 1968 < 1992 < 2012, so the order is Sensorama, head-mounted display, CAVE, Rift campaign.
Largest gap = 24 years, between the 1968 tracked display and the 1992 CAVE.

Contributions: Sensorama added multisensory presentation; the 1968 display added head tracking driving a computer-generated view; the CAVE added a room-sized view shared by several people; the Rift campaign added low-cost consumer head tracking with a wide field of view.
examples.answer: Order and years: Sensorama 1962, tracked head-mounted display 1968, CAVE 1992, Rift Kickstarter 2012; gaps are 6 years, 24 years and 20 years, so the largest gap is 24 years.
examples.check:
landmarks = [("Sensorama", 1962), ("Sutherland HMD", 1968), ("CAVE", 1992), ("Rift Kickstarter", 2012)]
landmarks.sort(key=lambda p: p[1])
for name, year in landmarks:
    print(year)
gaps = [landmarks[i+1][1] - landmarks[i][1] for i in range(len(landmarks) - 1)]
for g in gaps:
    print(g)
print(max(gaps))

traps: Giving one person everything. Sutherland built the first head-mounted display whose computer-generated image was driven by head tracking; Lanier's company VPL built the DataGlove and popularised the name; the CAVE came about two decades later.
Claiming VR was invented in the 2010s. The Rift campaign of 2012 revived an idea whose tracked head-mounted display already existed in 1968.
Calling the Sensorama a head-mounted display. It was a fixed booth for one seated person, with a recorded film and no head tracking.
Reading the Sword of Damocles as a product or a company. It is the nickname of one ceiling-hung laboratory rig, named for the arm and displays hanging over the user's head.
Mixing up the CAVE with a headset. The CAVE is a room of projection screens that several people can share without wearing a display.

quiz.q: Which device first showed two slightly different flat pictures, one to each eye, to produce depth, and in which year?
quiz.a: Wheatstone's stereoscope, 1838. Two drawings taken from viewpoints a little apart are fused by the brain into one scene with depth.

quiz.q: Who popularised the phrase virtual reality, and through which company?
quiz.a: Jaron Lanier, through VPL Research, in the 1980s. The same company built the DataGlove and the EyePhone.

quiz.q: Why is Sutherland's 1968 head-mounted display remembered as the Sword of Damocles?
quiz.a: Because the two small displays and the mechanical head tracker hung from the ceiling above the user. The nickname describes the suspended rig, not the software.

quiz.q: State one thing the Sensorama added and one thing it could not do.
quiz.a: It added multisensory presentation: stereo film, stereo sound, seat tilt and vibration, wind and smell in one booth. It could not respond to the viewer, because the film was fixed and there was no head tracking.

quiz.q: Place these in order and give the number of years from the first to the last: consumer headsets 2016, CAVE 1992, Sensorama 1962, Sutherland's tracked head-mounted display 1968.
quiz.a: Order by year: Sensorama 1962, tracked head-mounted display 1968, CAVE 1992, consumer headsets 2016. Span = 2016 − 1962 = 54 years.

quiz.q: Nintendo's Virtual Boy failed in 1995 while headsets sold in 2016. Give two differences that explain this.
quiz.a: Comfort: the Virtual Boy used a red monochrome display on a stand and was tiring to use, while 2016 headsets used colour displays with head tracking that matched the view to the head. Software and ecosystem: the Virtual Boy was a closed machine with only a couple of dozen titles, while the 2016 headsets had developer kits in programmers' hands for two years before launch, tracked hand controllers, and wide third-party software support. Cheap entry at that time came from phone-based viewers, not from the headsets themselves.

quiz.q: Name the three waves of VR history and say which barrier each one lowered.
quiz.a: Wave 1, before 1965: showed that depth comes from two correct flat views and that a machine can drive several senses and the body's sense of motion. Wave 2, 1965 to the 1990s: lowered the barrier of responsiveness by tracking the head and the hand, and gave the field its name and its room-sized shared view. Wave 3, from 2012: lowered the barrier of price and setup, with cheap sensors, wide fields of view, inside-out tracking and factory-scale production.

quiz.q: A lab buys a head-mounted display, a glove and a tracker in 1989 and wires them into one system for training. Which historical system does this most resemble, and what was it built for?
quiz.a: NASA's VIEW system of the late 1980s. It combined a head-mounted display, a glove, head tracking and the computer driving the scene in one machine for astronaut training and remote operation.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern headsets moved the tracking cameras onto the device and dropped external boxes; research now works on eye tracking, varifocal optics that focus where you look, and passthrough cameras that blend the real room into the virtual one (Unit 6). Open standards such as OpenXR let one application run on headsets from different makers, which is the current version of the old problem of hardware that does not talk to software. Useful search words: ultimate display 1965, VPL DataGlove history, CAVE automatic virtual environment, OpenXR.
